name: Khatso
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Donlay, Chris. 2015. A Functional Grammar of Khatso. PhD dissertation, University of California, Santa Barbara (UMI 3724770); author-posted PDF (khatso.net), 896 pp.
catalog_locator: Sec. 2.5.4 'Stress', pp. 149-151; domain sentence sec. 2.5.1 p. 140; sec. 2.6 intro p. 152; tones sec. 2.3.1 p. 98
catalog_quote: Stress, or accent, is not contrastive in Khatso at the word level. That is, there are no minimal pairs that are distinguished purely by different lexical stress patterns. Evidence for this conclusion is presented below. ... Unlike Putonghua, pitch is not a correlate of stress in Khatso. Because contours in different registers are already part of the lexical tone system, changing register alters meaning. ... An analysis of 90 disyllabic and trisyllabic responses obtained through elicitation, which include single as well as multiple word responses, fails to produce a predictable pattern involving the two features at the lexical level. ... None of the differences correlate with a specific lexical feature – segment, tone, syllable shape, syllable weight and word class are all irrelevant. ... As a result, the three features most likely to be used in lexical stress – pitch, intensity and duration – are not assigned at the word level in Khatso. Manipulating the pitch range of tone contours alters meaning, and thus is not an option for marking lexical stress. The remaining features, intensity and duration, pattern separately and, most importantly, randomly at the word level. Taken together, the evidence indicates that stress is not part of lexical phonology. Intensity and duration are used as IU boundary cues, however, as described in the next section.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Khatso is a tone language (eight lexical tones on every syllable) with no word-level stress: pitch is fully committed to lexical tone, and measured intensity and duration show no consistent word-level pattern across 90 elicited di-/trisyllabic tokens from two speakers. Prominence phenomena are phrasal: the intonation unit has an intensity peak on its first syllable and marked lengthening (lag) of its final syllable; 'Stress appears to be assigned at the phrase level rather than at the word level' (p. 140).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None; no lexical stress of any degree is posited.
new_statements.exceptions: None at word level. Author notes elicited citation forms show final-syllable lengthening, but demonstrates (noun vs noun+classifier) that lengthening targets the last syllable of the phrase/IU, not of the word; intensity peaks may fall on the first syllable of a syntactic constituent or a pragmatically emphasized element within longer IUs (sec. 2.6.4).
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly word-level negative statement backed by acoustic measurements of elicited forms; phrase/IU-level cues described separately (IU-initial intensity, IU-final lag). Same analysis restated in Donlay 2021 ICSTLL-54 slides ('Khatso does not have lexical stress') and, per the author's site, revised into Donlay 2019 A Grammar of Khatso ch. 4 (not opened).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Khatso as spoken in Xingmeng 兴蒙 township (the single Khatso-speaking community), Tonghai County, Yunnan = Glottolog kats1235 / ISO kaf (Katso, Kazhuo 卡卓/喀卓, Gazhuo 嘎卓); no dialect split. Fieldwork 2012-2014.

tone_statements.citation: Donlay, Chris. 2017. Multifunctionality in a tone sandhi pattern in Khatso. Paper presented at the 50th International Conference on Sino-Tibetan Languages and Linguistics (ICSTLL 50), Beijing, 26 November 2017. Abstract (2 pp.) and slides, Khatso Language Documentation Project, khatso.net/presentations.
tone_statements.quote: Khatso has eight contour tones: three level (55, 44, 33), two rising (35, 24), two falling (53, 31) and a low falling-rising tone (323). There are a number of unrelated sandhi patterns, but none are widespread. Instead, they occur in particular environments for specific purposes. However, one pattern is multifunctional; it occurs in different environments and requires context for differentiation. In this pattern, the syllable immediately preceding the trigger changes according to the following rule. If it carries tone 33 it changes to 44, if it is either tone 31 or 323 then it changes to 24; all other tones remain unaffected.
tone_statements.summary: 8 contour tones 55 44 33 35 24 53 31 323; TBU syllable; lexically/grammatically triggered sandhi 33>44, 31/323>24.

tone_statements.quote: It has eight contour tones: three level (55, 44, 33), two rising (35, 24), two falling (53, 31) and a low falling-rising tone (323). Every syllable carries a lexical tone, including grammatical particles; toneless syllables are not attested. Tone change in the language is not widespread. The most common pattern is triggered by a small set of words: the adverb to33 ‘also’, the dependent clause marker ni323, and the topic marker ni31.
tone_statements.summary: 8 contour tones 55 44 33 35 24 53 31 323; every syllable toned, no toneless syllables; lexically triggered sandhi 33>44, 31/323>24.
